items.title: Aplicação da inteligência artificial na gestão de riscos ocupacionais: análise crítica das oportunidades, limitações e responsabilidade técnica na engenharia de segurança do trabalho
items.abstract: RESUMO A incorporação da Inteligência Artificial (IA) na gestão da Saúde e Segurança do Trabalho (SST) amplia a identificação de perigos, o monitoramento ambiental e a análise preditiva de acidentes. Contudo, traz desafios técnicos, éticos e jurídicos sobre a confiabilidade dos dados e a responsabilidade profissional. Este estudo analisou criticamente o uso da IA no gerenciamento de riscos ocupacionais, mapeando suas oportunidades, limitações e impactos na atuação do Engenheiro de Segurança do Trabalho. Trata-se de uma revisão integrativa da literatura de natureza aplicada e abordagem qualitativa. Os resultados indicam que a IA possui elevado potencial analítico e operacional, mas apresenta riscos como alucinações, viés de automação e dependência da qualidade dos dados. Como contribuição, o estudo propõe um Framework de Governança pautado na supervisão humana obrigatória, validação técnica, transparência e responsabilidade profissional preservada sob supervisão humana. Conclui-se que a IA deve atuar estritamente como ferramenta de apoio, mantendo o protagonismo e a responsabilidade legal do especialista no processo decisório Palavras-chave: Inteligência Artificial. Engenharia de Segurança do Trabalho. Gestão de Riscos Ocupacionais. Prevenção de Acidentes. Governança da Inteligência Artificial. Responsabilidade Técnica. ABSTRACT The adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) management enhances hazard identification, environmental monitoring, and accident prediction. However, it raises technical, ethical, and legal challenges regarding data reliability and professional accountability. This study critically analyzed AI applications in occupational risk management, identifying opportunities, limitations, and impacts on Safety Engineers' technical responsibility. Developed as a qualitative, applied integrative literature review, the findings highlight AI's strong potential for data processing and continuous monitoring alongside critical limitations such as hallucinations, automation bias, and data dependency. As a primary contribution, the study proposes a Governance Framework based on mandatory human oversight, technical validation, algorithmic transparency, and non-transferable professional responsibility. It is concluded that AI must serve strictly as a decision-support tool, preserving the central role and legal responsibility of safety professionals. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence. Safety Engineering. Occupational Risk Management. Accident Prevention. Artificial Intelligence Governance. Technical Responsibility.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) FOR ACCOUNTING AND ANALYTICAL SUPPORT IN THE MANAGEMENT OF CROP PRODUCTION AND EXPORTS
items.abstract: The article examines the possibilities of using artificial intelligence in the system of accounting and analytical support for managing crop production and export operations. The relevance of the study is associated with the growing amount of accounting, production, logistics and foreign economic information that agribusiness enterprises need to process, particularly under the unstable conditions of the Ukrainian economy. The study identifies the main areas of AI application for automating accounting procedures, analyzing production costs, inventories and revenues, forecasting production indicators, detecting deviations, and supporting management decisions. Particular attention is paid to linking accounting data with information on crop yields, resource consumption, inventories, logistics, export contracts, settlements with counterparties and foreign currency transactions. Such integration provides a more complete basis for assessing production efficiency, determining the causes of changes in costs and financial results, and responding to deviations in a timely manner. An approach to integrating AI tools into the accounting and analytical system of agribusiness enterprises is proposed, taking into account the specific conditions of agricultural production and export activity in Ukraine. The study also considers the use of AI for processing primary and export documents, identifying inconsistencies between accounting and operational data, forecasting production costs and yields, and assessing the possible impact of logistics changes on export results. The main benefits and risks of AI use are outlined, including dependence on data quality, protection of confidential information, possible algorithmic errors, and excessive reliance on automated recommendations. It is emphasized that AI should complement rather than replace accounting procedures and professional judgement. The proposed approach can be used as a basis for further improvement of digital accounting and analytical systems in Ukrainian agribusiness enterprises and for strengthening information support for production and export management.

items.title: Artificial intelligence across community, mental and child health nursing: a future-ready framework for precision, preventive and person centered care
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare by enabling precision, predictive, and person-centered approaches that enhance the quality, accessibility, and efficiency of nursing care. Community, mental, and child health nursing are increasingly benefiting from AI-driven innovations, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, clinical decision support systems, wearable technologies, conversational AI, and telehealth platforms. These technologies facilitate early disease detection, population health surveillance, risk prediction, personalized interventions, remote patient monitoring, developmental screening, mental health assessment, and evidence-based clinical decision-making. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on the integration of AI across community, mental, and child health nursing and explores its implications for preventive healthcare, health promotion, and holistic patient management. Relevant literature published between 2018 and 2026 was identified through major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that AI improves healthcare accessibility, strengthens continuity of care, enhances diagnostic accuracy, supports personalized nursing interventions, and optimizes resource utilization. However, successful implementation requires addressing challenges related to ethical governance, algorithmic bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, interoperability, digital infrastructure, and AI competency among nurses. The review concludes that AI should function as a clinical decision-support tool that complements, rather than replaces, professional nursing judgment. Strategic investment in digital health education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible AI governance will be essential for developing future-ready nurses capable of delivering equitable, evidence-based, and compassionate healthcare across diverse populations.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Framework for Cybersecurity Resilience in Distributed Networks
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of distributed computer networks, driven by cloud computing, IoT ecosystems, edge computing, and software-defined infrastructures, has increased cybersecurity complexity. The growing volume, velocity, and variety of network data challenge traditional security mechanisms that focus primarily on threat detection, often neglecting system resilience, adaptive response, and recovery. This study develops a resilience-oriented intelligent big data analytics framework integrating Artificial Intelegence (AI), big data processing, and distributed cybersecurity monitoring to strengthen resilience in modern digital environments. A qualitative approach was employed through systematic literature review, conceptual modeling, thematic synthesis, and comparative analysis of existing architectures. The framework consists of four interconnected layers: data acquisition and aggregation, big data processing, intelligent analytics, and adaptive response and recovery. It supports continuous monitoring, anomaly detection, threat prediction, automated mitigation, and recovery orchestration. Comparative analysis indicates that prior studies focus mainly on improving intrusion detection or machine learning techniques, providing limited attention to resilience dimensions such as adaptability, fault tolerance, recovery efficiency, and operational stability. In contrast, the proposed framework integrates intelligent analytics with scalable big data infrastructures and distributed security mechanisms to create a unified resilience-oriented cybersecurity ecosystem. Findings suggest that combining AI-driven analytics, distributed processing, and adaptive security orchestration provides a strategic foundation for enhancing cybersecurity resilience, supporting sustainable digital infrastructure development, and ensuring operational stability in increasingly complex and interconnected network environments.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things-Based Food Authenticity and Adulteration Detection in Spices: A Review Paper
items.abstract: Culinary spices represent one of the most commonly adulterated agricultural commodities worldwide due to the complexity of their supply chain and the high economic value of the product. Traditional laboratory analyses (e.g., High-performance liquid chromatography, Mass spectrometry, and Wet chemical tests) are destructive, time-consuming, and insufficient for the high-throughput screening of spice powders or botanicals. This paper conducts a narrative literature review of 22 selected sources published between 2016 and 2026 that fall under seven themes: spice supply-chain risks and adulteration profiles, computer vision and deep learning approaches, portable Vis–NIR spectroscopy, electronic nose and gas sensing, multi-sensor fusion and chemometric analysis, machine learning methods for quantifying adulteration concentrations, and Edge-IoT hardware solutions. The reviewed articles demonstrate that Convolutional Neural Networks and transfer learning can reach an excellent level of precision in distinguishing between whole spices and botanical intruders, while compact Vis-NIR spectral sensors can detect food dyes and starch fillers in ground powders. SVM/Random Forest classifier-based MOS gas-sensor arrays can detect spoiled spices and vision-spectral fusion can have more accurate detection than a single modality. Nevertheless, most of the data presented in the literature is based on experiments performed on an oversimplified scenario of adulteration, and there are not enough publicly available multi-modal sensor datasets. This research presents a thematic literature review, a comparison of features in fourteen selected papers, a proposed conceptual framework, and recommendations.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and school leadership in inclusive organisational processes.
items.abstract: This article offers a theoretical and methodological reflection on the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and school leadership, on the assumption that the spread of intelligent systems constitutes an epistemological transformation capable of redefining educational governance, decision-making processes and school organisation. In line with the paradigm of complexity (Morin, 2001), innovation is not interpreted as the mere introduction of digital tools, but as a redefinition of the categories through which schools observe, interpret and govern the educational reality. AI therefore represents a pedagogical challenge even before it is a technological one, requiring leadership capable of integrating organisational, ethical, pedagogical and technological dimensions, and orienting them towards equity, participation and inclusion (Fullan, 2014). From this perspective, education continues to be aimed at human development (Biesta, 2022) and the expansion of people's capabilities (Nussbaum, 2011). items.title: Artificial intelligence and SDGs, a friend or foe: A perspective of Kantianism
items.abstract: Humans have keen interests with artificial objects. We consume food and drinks containing artificial coloring while FIFA approves the use of artificial turf for football matches. However, the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has gripped the world with its radical changes, triggering not only physical, but also philosophical implications. In this paper, we explore the impact of AI on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and pose the question of whether the human centrality of the SDGs could diminish with the introduction of AI. Drawing on Kant’s concept of universalism and categorical imperatives, we argue that AI cannot safeguard intergenerational justice or meet Kant’s definition of a rational being. This paper presents a brief yet significant perspective, emphasizing the need for caution when integrating AI into the implementation of the SDGs, particularly concerning policy design.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as a supportive agent in the crafting of terminology development
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a supportive agent in professional terminology work, using the Estonian national defence terminology as a case study. The study addresses the growing need to manage large volumes of multilingual defence-related documentation while simultaneously preserving expert-driven, concept-oriented terminology development practices. We present and evaluate a retrieval-augmented, large language model (LLM)-based prototype designed to extract and structure source-grounded (English) terminological raw material — such as definition candidates, related terms, usage contexts, and exact references — rather than to generate dictionary-ready entries. The prototype was evaluated through an expert-based assessment involving both domain specialists and experienced terminologists. The evaluation focused on the practical usefulness, contextual adequacy, and completeness of the extracted information, rather than on formal definitional correctness alone. The results indicate that the prototype performs reliably in retrieving definition candidates, contextual evidence, and source references, and can meaningfully support the early stages of terminology work. At the same time, persistent limitations were identified, including occasional hallucinations under weak source constraints, inconsistent handling of semantic relations, and challenges at the boundary between general and specialised language. The findings underscore the continued centrality of human expertise in terminology development and support a human-at-the-core model — as distinct from a human-in-the-loop model, where humans primarily correct machine output — in which AI functions as an assistive, context-sensitive tool rather than an autonomous terminological agent. The study contributes contextualised empirical evidence to ongoing debates on AI-assisted terminology management and offers methodological insights into prompt design, expert evaluation, and the integration of AI tools into institutional terminology workflows, particularly in small-language and national defence contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Patient Information Tools: A Bilingual, Two-Round Evaluation of the e-Nabız Personal Health Record System
items.abstract: This study evaluated four widely used large language models—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek—as patient-information tools for e-Nabız, the national personal health record system of Türkiye, and tested whether their answers were reproducible one week apart. Thirty authentic patient questions spanning seven e-Nabız domains were submitted to each model in Turkish and English, in fresh sessions with default settings, and the protocol was repeated after one week (480 responses). A dated copy of the official e-Nabız User Guide served as the gold standard, and responses were scored blind for accuracy, completeness, the Global Quality Score, coverage, and safety, with readability computed using the Flesch, Flesch–Kincaid, Ateşman, and Bezirci–Yılmaz formulas. Model performance differed significantly in both languages, with Claude and Gemini outperforming ChatGPT and DeepSeek; two models performed better in Turkish. All models wrote above recommended reading levels, and although aggregate quality was stable between rounds, individual answers were substantially reworded and sometimes materially changed. Chatbots should complement, not replace, official e-Nabız guidance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Driving the Transformation of Modern Libraries
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping the operations, services, and user engagement strategies of modern libraries, including those in higher education and public domains. AI technologies, encompassing machine learning, natural language processing, chatbots, and predictive analytics, enable libraries to automate routine tasks, personalize information services, and generate data-driven insights for collection development and resource management. This paper examines the role of AI in modern libraries, focusing on three core dimensions: automation of cataloguing, classification, and reference services; intelligent discovery and personalized recommendation systems; and AI-driven analytics for decision-making and user engagement. The paper reviews the conceptual architecture of AI-enabled library systems, surveys current applications, and discusses the institutional, ethical, and technical challenges associated with adoption. It concludes by outlining future directions, including the convergence ofAI withIoTand cloud computing, forbuilding intelligent, adaptive library ecosystems.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in corporate legal risk management: A governance and accountability framework
items.abstract: The acceleration of the regulatory requirement, globalization of operations and digital transformation has increased the corporate vulnerability to legal risk. The current legal risk management methods which are mostly reactive and manual fail to handle the scale and complexity of the modern legal and compliance issues. Corporations are in turn moving towards artificial intelligence (AI) more and more as a method of improving legal risk identification, evaluation, and reduction. The paper explores the ways of using AI to balance the control of corporate legal risk and governance, accountability, and ethical responsibility. Using a qualitative and conceptual research of the existing literature, the study examines the major types of corporate legal risk such as regulatory compliance, contractual risk, litigation exposure, governance failures, and data protection issues. The paper examines AI applications within the corporate legal functions, including natural language processing, machine learning, and predictive analytics, and puts into the limelight, how these applications can be used to facilitate proactive and predictive risk management. Meanwhile, the paper critically considers the issues related to the use of AI such as algorithmic bias, transparency, threats to privacy, and legal accountability ambiguity. To resolve the challenges a conceptual framework is suggested, which incorporates the AI capabilities in the corporate level of legal risk management in a regulation-focused and ethically sound framework. The article adds to the literature because it offers a comprehensive view of AI-sensitive law risk management and offers useful data that corporations should consider in terms of finding the balance between innovation and legal accountability.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Endodontics: A Narrative Review and Critical Synthesis of Diagnostic, Predictive, and Operational Applications
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) research in endodontics has grown quickly, but the strength of the evidence differs between applications. This narrative review with structured evidence mapping examined diagnostic imaging, canal morphology, outcome prediction, large language models (LLMs), robotics and augmented reality, and operational uses such as case-difficulty assessment, triage and scheduling. Methods: Two anchor reviews were combined with a documented PubMed search to 30 September 2026, and studies were classified by design, sample, reference standard, validation, and evidence of clinical utility. Results: Periapical lesion detection has the largest evidence base: one meta-analysis reported pooled sensitivity of 0.925 and specificity of 0.852, although most included studies were at risk of bias and none was prospective. Fracture detection relies mainly on ex vivo data and is sensitive to image resolution. Outcome models showed modest to moderate discrimination in single-centre data. LLM studies reported 40% to 100% correct, appropriate, or concordant responses across different benchmarks and scoring rules, and outputs varied on repeated querying. Difficulty-assessment and scheduling tools have appeared since 2020 but have not been evaluated prospectively in clinical workflow. Conclusions: Technical performance has not yet been shown to translate into clinical benefit, and AI in endodontics should currently be used only as clinician-supervised decision support.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Assessing Patient Protection Under Law No. 17 of 2023 and Article 28H, Paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare presents significant legal challenges concerning patient safety, data protection, and medical accountability. This study examines the adequacy of Indonesia's constitutional and statutory frameworks in protecting patients receiving AI-assisted healthcare services and identifies regulatory measures necessary to strengthen legal certainty. Employing a normative juridical approach, the research analyzes Article 28H(1) of the 1945 Constitution, Law No. 17 of 2023 concerning Health, and Law No. 27 of 2022 concerning Personal Data Protection through statutory, conceptual, and doctrinal legal analysis. The findings demonstrate that existing regulations provide a substantive foundation for patient rights, informed consent, professional responsibility, and medical data confidentiality. However, significant regulatory limitations remain regarding algorithmic transparency, clinical validation, continuous performance monitoring, human oversight, and the allocation of liability among healthcare professionals, institutions, and technology providers. The study argues that these limitations reflect insufficient operational specificity rather than a complete legal vacuum. Accordingly, it proposes an integrated, risk-based regulatory framework incorporating AI-specific clinical safeguards, transparent decision-making, strengthened data governance, and clearly defined accountability mechanisms. This research contributes to the development of Indonesian healthcare law by demonstrating how existing constitutional guarantees and statutory obligations can be operationalized to ensure patient protection while supporting responsible AI innovation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in innovation activities: Firm practices and managerial perspectives in Kazakhstan
items.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in innovation activities, yet firm-level evidence on variation across innovation stages and organizational conditions remains limited in emerging economies such as Kazakhstan. This study examines AI use among surveyed firms in Kazakhstan, focusing on stage-specific influence, organizational correlates, barriers, reported effects, and managerial perceptions. A cross-sectional voluntary survey yielded a non-probability sample of 93 firms; data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests, exploratory bivariate analysis, multinomial logistic regression, and descriptive review of open-ended recommendations. In the sample, 39.8% reported no AI use in innovation activities; 23.7% used AI frequently or always. Idea generation was rated higher than idea testing and selection (r = .398), although concordance in stage rankings was weak (Kendall’s W = .077). The reported AI-related resource-category count was associated with both occasional (RRR = 6.98) and frequent AI use (RRR = 7.10) relative to no reported AI use in innovation activities. At the same time, firm size and age were not significant. Skills shortages, financial constraints, regulatory uncertainty, and ethical concerns were the leading barriers. Among firms reporting AI use in innovation activities, the most frequently reported effects were greater innovation-process efficiency (46.4%) and improved understanding of industry opportunities and trends (30.4%). items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Software Engineering: From Code Generation to Reasoning
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most influential technologies shaping software engineering in recent years. This transformation has moved beyond early code generation and completion tools toward systems capable of participating in requirements analysis, design, testing, debugging, documentation, and solving complex software problems. The aim of this review paper is to examine the evolving role of AI in software engineering, with a particular focus on the transition from code generation tools to reasoning-based infrastructures. In this study, relevant research and studies on the application of Large Language Models (LLMs), code generation tools, and intelligent systems across different phases of the software development lifecycle are reviewed and categorized. The distinction between automatic code generation and capabilities such as problem analysis, planning, multi-step reasoning, and solution evaluation is also discussed. Findings from the reviewed literature indicate that AI can evolve from an auxiliary tool for generating code fragments into an effective factor in supporting more complex software engineering processes. However, issues such as output correctness, reasoning errors, code security, dependence on training data, trustworthiness, and the necessity of human oversight remain significant challenges in this field. Finally, the paper emphasizes the need to move from a purely "code generation" perspective toward a more comprehensive approach based on human–AI collaboration in software engineering processes.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Intergenerational Transmission of Religious Values: New Challenges for the Family and Upbringing from the Perspective of Catholic Personalist Anthropology
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the environments in which religious questions are explored, and values are interpreted and transmitted across generations. Although existing scholarship addresses digital religion and the ethical and educational implications of AI, the mechanisms through which conversational AI may influence intergenerational religious communication within families require further conceptual examination. This article develops a Responsible Relational AI Mediation Model grounded in family pedagogy, religious socialization theory, digital religion studies, AI ethics, and Catholic personalist anthropology. This study employs an interdisciplinary conceptual approach based on critical literature analysis and synthesis, supplemented by selected international policy documents and Catholic Church teaching. The proposed model integrates three analytical dimensions: structural, identifying the persons, relationships, communities, and technologies involved in religious formation; processual, examining how AI-generated interpretations may influence perceived authority and intergenerational dialogue; and normative, establishing criteria for responsible technological mediation. It distinguishes between relationally integrated and non-integrated pathways of AI-mediated religious inquiry and recognizes generative AI as an educational tool, a mediator of interpretation, and a potential environment for ongoing religious learning. This article argues that the formative significance of AI depends on how its use is connected with critical discernment, interpersonal relationships, and religious community participation. The model offers a conceptual framework for future empirical research rather than establishing causal effects of AI on religious formation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management for Nursing Organisations: A Concept Analysis
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in nursing management through workforce modelling, quality surveillance, resource allocation and organisational decision support. However, artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management remains conceptually underdeveloped, particularly regarding governance, accountability and nursing-specific leadership responsibilities. Objective: To analyse and define artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management and develop a conceptual framework for future empirical research, competency development and responsible AI implementation. Design: A concept analysis using Walker and Avant’s eight-step methodology, supported by a structured search to identify conceptually relevant interdisciplinary literature. Setting: Peer-reviewed interdisciplinary literature and authoritative policy and professional guidance documents identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, Europe PMC, ProQuest Nursing & Allied Health Database and relevant authoritative sources, published between 2020 and 2025. Main outcome measures: Defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, model cases and empirical referents. Results: Twenty-four substantive sources were retained for conceptual analysis; methodological and theoretical foundations were used separately to guide analysis and support theoretical positioning. Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management was conceptualised as a governance-specialised extension of nursing leadership comprising five interrelated attributes: strategic AI direction-setting, managerial AI literacy, ethical and regulatory oversight, organisational change leadership and workforce capability development, and systematic integration into nursing management processes. Antecedents were organised as core or contextual conditions; consequences were differentiated into proximal and proposed distal consequences, the latter requiring empirical validation. Empirical referents were identified at individual, workforce and organisational levels. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management clarifies the leadership responsibilities required when AI informs nursing managerial decision-making, including algorithmic accountability, human oversight and preservation of professional nursing judgement. The concept provides a foundation for competency development, empirical validation and organisational governance across health and aged care settings, including Asia-Pacific contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Financial Services and Fintech
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports financial decision-making, risk assessment, service innovation, and customer interaction. This study maps the Web of Science (WoS) -indexed literature on AI technologies in financial services and financial technology (FinTech) through a PRISMA-guided bibliometric analysis of 512 English-language articles published from 2016 to 2025. Performance analysis, VOSviewer co-word mapping, CiteSpace timeline analysis, and keyword burst detection are combined to examine publication patterns, research contributors, thematic structure, and changes in scholarly attention. The selected corpus shows rapid publication growth and three prominent co-word domains: AI-driven FinTech innovation, machine learning for credit risk and fraud detection, and user adoption of digital financial services. Temporal mapping and the recent burst of the keyword 'trust' indicate increasing scholarly interest in governance-related and user-oriented concerns, alongside established technical applications. These trends also highlight the relevance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations, particularly AI sustainability, financial inclusion, and responsible governance. Drawing on these observed patterns, the study advances a socio-technical interpretation in which trustworthy AI governance is proposed as a conceptual linkage among innovation, risk management, and user adoption. The framework is an interpretive synthesis, not an empirically validated causal model. Because the study uses a predefined WoS-only search without formal cross-database or search-strategy sensitivity testing, the findings apply to the selected corpus and should not be regarded as exhaustive of the global literature. The resulting research agenda emphasises responsible management of information resources in AI-enabled financial services.

items.title: Artificial intelligence tools for developing research and academic writing skills among graduate students: An action research study
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed higher education by providing tools that support research and academic writing. This action research study examined changes in graduate students' research and academic writing outcomes following a structured six-week instructional intervention integrating Perplexity AI and Jenni AI. Seventeen graduate students participated in workshops on the effective and ethical use of both tools. Data were collected using pre- and post-intervention questionnaires and an analytical rubric evaluating students' research papers. The mean rubric score increased from 62.51 (SD = 9.80) to 86.47 (SD = 6.59) out of 100, t (16) = 8.26, p < .001, 95% CI [17.81, 30.10], Cohen's dz = 2.00. The overall questionnaire mean increased from 3.17 (SD = 0.56) to 4.42 (SD = 0.51) on a five-point Likert scale, t (16) = 7.99, p < .001, 95% CI [0.92, 1.59], Cohen's dz = 1.94. Participation in the structured AI-supported intervention was associated with substantial improvements in research-paper performance and self-reported research, writing, and AI-related outcomes. The findings also underscore the importance of ethical use, critical evaluation, and human oversight. Given the small single-group design, the results should be interpreted as evidence of pre–post change rather than proof of a causal effect attributable to either AI tool.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted cytology improves diagnostic consistency and accuracy in cervical cancer screening: A multicenter crossover study
items.abstract: Objectives: The effective prevention and control of cervical cancer (CC) depend on high-quality screening. However, traditional cytology interpretation faces challenges such as strong subjectivity, significant inter-observer variability, and a shortage of cytopathologists in primary care settings. The distribution of high-quality medical resources in China is highly uneven between urban and rural areas. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cytology offers a new approach to enhance screening efficacy. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a deep learning-based AI-assisted cytology system in a multicenter clinical environment in China, comparing its utility as a standalone tool and in a collaborative model with cytopathologists. Materials and Methods: This was a multicenter, crossover study enrolling a total of 769 outpatient liquid-based cytology samples obtained from three participating hospitals. Using a crossover design, two junior-to-mid-level cytopathologists from primary hospitals performed independent diagnoses and AI-assisted diagnoses (following an AI preliminary screening combined with cytopathologist verification), which were compared with AI-alone diagnoses. Using an expert cytology panel diagnosis as the cytological reference standard, sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), overall accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV) negative predictive value, and false-positive rates/false-negative rates and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated and compared for each modality at the atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US+), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL+), and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+) thresholds. Results: The study found that the independent diagnostic Se of the primary cytopathologists was insufficient (LSIL+: 46.0% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.359–0.564)–50.6% (95% CI: 0.403–0.608); HSIL+: 36.6% (95% CI: 0.236–0.519)–46.3% (95% CI: 0.321–0.613), indicating a high risk of missed diagnoses. AI-alone diagnosis showed high Se (ASC-US+: 92.9% [95% CI: 0.877–0.960]) but a relatively lower PPV (72.0% [95% CI: 0.654–0.778]). AI-assisted diagnostic model achieved a favorable balance. Across all diagnostic thresholds, the AI-assisted modality significantly outperformed cytopathologist-alone diagnosis. At the ASC-US+ threshold, AI-alone Se was 92.9% (95% CI: 0.877–0.960) with a Sp of 90.9% (95% CI: 0.883–0.929), whereas the sensitivities of the two primary cytopathologists alone were 68.4% (95% CI: 0.607–0.752) and 81.3% (95% CI: 0.744–0.866), respectively. With AI assistance, primary cytopathologist Se increased to 92.3% (95% CI: 0.870–0.955)–94.2% (95% CI: 0.893–0.969), and Sp reached 94.6% (95% CI: 0.925–0.961)–96.9% (95% CI: 0.952–0.980). At the LSIL+ and HSIL+ thresholds, where cytopathologist-alone sensitivities were low (LSIL+: 46.0% [95% CI: 0.359–0.564]–50.6% [95% CI: 0.403–0.608]; HSIL+: 36.6% [95% CI: 0.236–0.519]–46.3% [95% CI: 0.321–0.613]), AI assistance improved them to 80.5% (95% CI: 0.709–0.874) and 73.2% (95% CI: 0.581–0.843)–75.6% (95% CI: 0.607–0.862), respectively, with Sp exceeding 97.0% in both cases. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis confirmed that the AUC for AI-assisted diagnosis (0.938 [95% CI: 0.911–0.965]–0.971 [95% CI: 0.946–0.996]) was significantly higher than that for cytopathologist-alone diagnosis (0.791 [95% CI: 0.746–0.836]–0.868 [95% CI: 0.819–0.918]). Conclusion: In this exploratory study, the AI-assisted cytology system may help reduce the experience gap for primary cytopathologists in primary hospitals, substantially improving the Se and Sp of cervical cytology interpretation. The AI-assisted diagnostic model is an effective strategy for achieving standardized, high-quality CC screening, particularly for promoting homogeneous services in regions with uneven healthcare resources.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven educational technology innovation and sustainable digital transformation: Patent-based evidence on global technological inequality
items.abstract: Abstract Equitable digital education is central to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). Yet as digital systems shape how education is delivered, assessed and governed, a deeper divide is emerging between countries that can merely adopt educational technologies and those that can develop, adapt and govern them. This study examines the global distribution of technology-shaping capacity in education using 274,825 educational-technology patent records filed from 2006 to 2025. We combine four-period spatial mapping, concentration measures, 16 technology themes, annual trajectories, and LightGBM-SHAP interpretation of high-value patents from 2013 to 2023. Geographic participation expanded after 2011, yet inventive activity remained strongly concentrated: the leading country accounted for 63.48–77.62% of records across the three mature periods, while the five leading countries consistently exceeded 90%. Innovation shifted from stand-alone teaching tools toward virtual reality, artificial intelligence, adaptive learning, platform-based services and data-intensive systems. Geographic, technological and temporal variables contributed 33.33%, 27.03% and 25.78%, respectively, to the prediction of high-value patents, and high-value inventions were concentrated in a limited set of country-theme pathways. These patterns reveal a capability divide overlooked by connectivity indicators. Education systems may gain access to advanced tools without gaining the capacity to adapt them to local languages and curricula, audit algorithms, govern data or develop alternatives. By revealing where technology-shaping capacity and high-value innovation are concentrated, this study can help policymakers identify priorities for capability building, technology transfer and governance support to advance more inclusive and sustainable digital transformation toward SDG 4.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled detection of vascular perfusion defects on ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy for pulmonary embolism
items.abstract: Abstract Objective:Accurate interpretation of planar ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, used for diagnosing pulmonary embolism (PE) based on PIOPED/EANM guidelines, requires objective assessment of mismatched V/Q defects. Manual delineation of V/Q defects is time-consuming, subject to interobserver variability, and rarely performed in practice, limiting standardized reporting and quantification of disease burden. To address these challenges, we evaluated four modern AI models for automated segmentation of vascular perfusion defects in planar V/Q scans and compared their performance to human annotators.Approach:We retrospectively identified 2,118 patients who underwent planar V/Q scans at The Ottawa Hospital (June 2019-February 2023). Six standard projections (ANT, POST, LAO, RAO, LPO, RPO) were included. Four 2D neural networks (U-Net, nnU-Net, Swin UNETR, and a Bottleneck Transformer U-Net [BTU-Net]) were trained on 1,313 patients (7,878 projections) and validated on 329 (1,974 projections) using physician-annotated defects. A hold-out test set of 46 high probability patients was used to evaluate segmentation quality, and defect detection accuracy using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) analysis.Main results:BTU-Net was the only model performing on par with human readers, showing robust sensitivity across the entire range of segmentation probabilities. At 1.5 false positives per projection rate (FPPR), BTU-Net outperformed other models with sensitivity of 0.529 ± 0.026, On a separate hold-out set of low likelihood of disease patients (n=430), the lowest FPPR was 0.08 ± 0.01 for BTU-Net (P<0.0001).Significance:BTU-Net enables rapid, consistent, and accurate interpretation of planar V/Q scans. Such tools may enhance diagnostic efficiency, standardize reporting, and support non-expert readers in evaluating PE.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Automated Optical Coherence Tomography Analysis for Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Planning: From Plaque Analysis to Precision Lesion Preparation and Stent Optimization
items.abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains the cornerstone of revascularization in coronary artery disease. However, despite advances in stent technology, adverse outcomes related to suboptimal stent placement including under-expansion, malapposition, incomplete coverage, edge dissection, and neoatherosclerosis persist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the highest resolution widely available intravascular imaging modality, allowing unparalleled visualization of stent-vessel interactions and plaque morphology. However, there are significant barriers to large-scale OCT adoption, including time-consuming manual interpretation and dependence on the operator, resulting in significant variability between analysts. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated OCT analysis promises to assist PCI by delivering rapid, reproducible, and standardized stent optimization, but current analysis systems lack important features to optimize stent placement. This review summarizes the principles of OCT in PCI, the evidence for OCT-guided optimization, and recent advances in AI-driven automated OCT analysis. We discuss plaque analysis and classification, highlighting how AI-driven automated OCT analysis can identify fibrous, lipid-rich, and calcified lesions and guide tailored lesion preparation using balloons, specialty balloons, drug-coated balloons, intravascular lithotripsy, and atherectomy. We outline emerging AI-enabled workflows for fully automated PCI optimization, evaluate clinical outcomes, interpretability, and workflow integration. Finally, we explore future directions including AI imaging-physiology fusion, multiomics integration, and robotics. If successful, automated AI-empowered OCT analysis could become a central imaging platform for precision PCI, enabling tailored lesion preparation, optimal stent deployment, and improved clinical outcomes in coronary artery disease management.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence–Supported Patient Navigation Addressing Social Drivers of Health among Vulnerable Adults in Family Medicine and Geriatrics Safety-Net Clinics
items.abstract: Abstract: Health-related social needs such as housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are associated with worse health outcomes and increased health care utilization, particularly among older adults. Although health systems increasingly screen for these needs, many lack the capacity to provide follow-up support at scale. This pilot evaluation described the implementation and early operational performance of an artificial intelligence-supported, on-demand patient navigation service integrated into an urban safety-net health system. From July 2024 to March 2025, providers placed 149 referrals from family medicine and geriatrics clinics. Outreach was attempted for all referred patients, and successful contact occurred for 78 patients. Navigators submitted 301 applications for public benefits and community resources; 145 were approved, while others remained pending or in process at analysis. Program costs during the observation period were approximately $5,000. These findings suggest feasibility while highlighting the need for further evaluation of patient experience and outcomes.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, emotional well-being, and difficult dialogues in school settings
items.abstract: Attention to students' emotional dimension represents a key determinant of both academic success and future personal and social development (Weber et al., 2016). Within this perspective, the design of emotionally meaningful learning experiences, including those supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based conversational technologies, can enhance students' well-being and engagement by recognizing emotions as a fundamental component of learning processes. Through Natural Language Processing techniques and affective computing models, intelligent conversational systems can detect and interpret users' emotional states and dynamically adapt interactions accordingly. In particular, so-called empathic conversational agents (Ortega-Ochoa et al., 2024) are artificial entities designed to elicit empathic responses from users (Hall & Woods, 2006) and to generate highly personalized simulated environments by modulating content, feedback, and task difficulty according to identified emotional factors. Such artificial conversations enable learners to engage in adaptive learning experiences in which their emotional state becomes an active variable in the regulation of the educational pathway. items.title: As effective as the teacher, but less motivating: a randomized controlled comparison of AI-generated and teacher feedback on students’ writing performance and intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

items.title: Aspectos éticos de la inteligencia artificial en las instituciones de educación superior
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence is generating rapid transformations in society and, particularly, in higher education institutions. Its incorporation offers significant opportunities for teaching and learning processes, but it also raises challenges related to academic integrity, privacy, bias, authorship, equity, plagiarism, and the generation of false information. This reflective essay aims to analyze the main ethical aspects associated with the use of artificial intelligence in higher education institutions and to highlight the responsibilities of the different actors within the educational community. Methodologically, the study adopted a qualitative, documentary, and reflective approach based on the critical analysis of recent scientific literature and documents from international organizations addressing ethics and the use of artificial intelligence in educational contexts. The analysis highlights the need to establish clear institutional policies, regulations, and guidelines that promote the ethical, transparent, and responsible use of these technologies. It is concluded that higher education institutions play a fundamental role in regulating their use, educating students and faculty, and promoting continuous ethical reflection to ensure that technological innovation is aligned with academic integrity, the protection of rights, and human responsibility.

items.title: Assédio moral no trabalho no contexto das instituições militares estaduais
items.abstract: RESUMO O assédio moral constitui forma de violência psicológica capaz de degradar o ambiente de trabalho, comprometer a saúde do trabalhador e afetar a eficiência institucional. Nas Polícias Militares e nos Corpos de Bombeiros Militares estaduais, a análise do fenômeno exige especial cautela, porque o exercício legítimo da autoridade convive com estruturas rígidas de hierarquia e disciplina. Este artigo examina os elementos caracterizadores do assédio moral, suas formas de manifestação e suas consequências, distinguindo-o do poder regular de comando, fiscalização e correção. Adota-se pesquisa qualitativa, bibliográfica e documental, com análise da Constituição Federal, da Lei nº 6.880/1980, da Lei nº 14.751/2023, do Código Penal Militar, de proposições legislativas e de literatura especializada. Sustenta-se que hierarquia e disciplina não autorizam humilhação, perseguição, discriminação ou desvio de finalidade. Embora ainda não exista tipo penal federal específico e vigente de assédio moral no Código Penal Militar, o fato pode produzir responsabilização civil, administrativa e, conforme as circunstâncias, penal. Conclui-se que a prevenção depende de liderança ética, canais protegidos de denúncia, apuração imparcial, proteção contra retaliações, formação continuada e acompanhamento da saúde ocupacional, sem enfraquecimento dos fundamentos constitucionais das instituições militares. Palavras-chave: assédio moral; militares estaduais; hierarquia; disciplina; abuso de poder; saúde ocupacional. ABSTRACT Workplace bullying is a form of psychological violence capable of degrading the work environment, harming workers' health and impairing institutional effectiveness. In State Military Police and State Military Fire Brigades, its assessment requires particular caution because legitimate authority operates within rigid structures of hierarchy and discipline. This article examines the defining elements, manifestations and consequences of workplace bullying, distinguishing it from lawful command, supervision and correction. It adopts a qualitative, bibliographic and documentary approach based on the Federal Constitution, Federal Laws No. 6,880/1980 and No. 14,751/2023, the Military Criminal Code, legislative proposals and specialized literature. The study argues that hierarchy and discipline do not authorize humiliation, persecution, discrimination or misuse of authority. Although no specific and effective federal criminal offense of workplace bullying currently exists in the Military Criminal Code, abusive conduct may result in civil, administrative and, depending on the circumstances, criminal liability. Prevention requires ethical leadership, protected reporting channels, impartial investigations, safeguards against retaliation, continuing education and occupational health monitoring, without weakening the constitutional foundations of military institutions. Keywords: workplace bullying; state military personnel; hierarchy; discipline; abuse of authority; occupational health.

items.title: Assessment of Occupational Health and Safety Needs in U.S. Public Health Region 6: National Implications for Research, Training, and Outreach
items.abstract: Objective. Assess occupational health and safety (OHS) workforce needs across Public Health Region 6 (PHR 6)—Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas—to identify gaps, priorities, and capacity-building opportunities and to inform national OHS priorities. Methods. A mixed-methods needs assessment integrated stakeholder engagement, national OHS professional and alumni surveys, federal dataset analysis, Education and Research Center (ERC) program records, literature review, and job market surveillance. Results. Demand for OHS professionals is projected to grow, particularly for safety specialists and industrial hygienists. Key unmet needs include mental health, workplace violence prevention, and exposure assessment. PHR 6 also experiences high occupational fatality rates and climate-related environmental burdens. Conclusions. Sustained investment in workforce development, interdisciplinary training, and outreach is essential to advance worker health equity and inform national OHS priorities.

items.title: Asymmetric Dependency and the Algorithmic Figuration
items.abstract: This article argues that AI-governed systems, and large language models in particular, introduce a novel dynamic into contemporary figurations: one of asymmetric dependency, in which people are materially, and increasingly affectively, dependent upon systems that are not, in turn, affectively dependent upon them. This condition attenuates the affectively reciprocal interdependency on which psychogenetic processes depend in Norbert Elias’s account of the civilising process and gives rise to what we distinguish as behavioural civilising: the shaping of observable conduct through monitored compliance rather than through the internalisation of restraint. Because such systems simulate human exchange whilst stripping it of its negative social consequences, they simultaneously suspend the shame functions through which figurational pressure is ordinarily converted into self-restraint and so exert decivilising pressures within the same figuration. Extended engagement with conversational AI also introduces generative reflection: a mode of exchange in which thought is elaborated and transformed rather than merely returned. We thereby extend the Eliasian framework whilst specifying the conditions under which psychogenetic processes are disrupted and transformed.

items.title: Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in Teacher Education: The Contribution of Cognitive and Emotional Variables
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational contexts is profoundly transforming teaching and learning processes, creating new opportunities for personalized instruction while simultaneously raising pedagogical, ethical, and professional challenges (Chen et al., 2020; ZawackiRichter et al., 2019). While traditional technology acceptance models have primarily emphasized the role of digital competencies and perceived usefulness (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003), more recent studies suggest that AI adoption is also shaped by emotional factors, including anxiety, distrust, fears of professional replacement, and concerns about the quality of the educational relationship (Schepman & Rodway, 2020; Liu & Liu, 2025). Within this framework, the present study investigates the combined contribution of cognitive and emotional factors to the development of attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence, assuming that AI acceptance is a multidimensional process in which knowledge, competencies, and emotional experiences interact dynamically. items.title: Audit transformation in the era of artificial intelligence: an integrative literature review of AI’s impact on audit quality, professional skepticism, and auditor competence
items.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the external audit, focusing on three linked outcomes: audit quality, auditors' professional skepticism, and the competences auditors need. Design/methodology/approach – An integrative literature review of 18 peer-reviewed studies in accounting, auditing and information systems published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by recent standard-setting documents from the IAASB and the PCAOB. Studies are coded by AI application, audit phase, research method and outcome, and synthesised thematically. Findings – AI extends audit coverage from samples to full populations and improves anomaly detection, fraud prediction, the evaluation of estimates and the efficiency of routine procedures. Archival evidence links AI investment by audit firms to fewer restatements, lower fees and more accurate going-concern and internal control opinions. However, the benefits depend on the human–machine relationship: auditors may discount AI evidence (algorithm aversion) or accept it without sufficient challenge (automation bias), and both can impair judgment. Model opacity, data quality, accountability and limited guidance in auditing standards remain unresolved risks, although standard setters have begun to respond. Research limitations – The review is integrative rather than systematic, covers English-language studies only and relies mainly on evidence from the United States, Europe and large audit firms. Evidence on generative AI in auditing is still at an early stage. Implications – Audit firms should treat AI output as evidence to be evaluated, design workflows that prompt challenge and protect the development of junior staff. Standard setters should clarify how much assurance AI-based procedures provide, and educators should combine data analytics with judgment training. Originality – The review integrates technical, behavioural and institutional strands into a single framework in which AI is proposed to affect audit quality mainly through calibrated professional skepticism and auditor competence. It derives five testable propositions and a research agenda relevant to both developed and emerging audit markets.

items.title: Authenticity of Islamic Religious Education: Actualization of Mindful, Meaningful, and Joyful Principles in Moral Learning at Elementary Schools
items.abstract: The authenticity of Islamic Religious Education in elementary schools faces significant contemporary challenges, shifting from transformative character building toward mechanical cognitive memorization. This study aims to re-actualize the core principles of authentic moral learning through a mindful, meaningful, and joyful paradigm tailored for elementary school students. Using a literature study approach with critical-qualitative analysis, this research examines classical and contemporary pedagogical frameworks to synthesize an integrated moral education model. The findings indicate that mindful learning enhances students' self-awareness and spiritual presence, meaningful learning connects religious doctrines with daily life experiences, and joyful learning fosters intrinsic motivation and emotional well-being. Synthesizing these three elements restores the authenticity of IRE, transforming moral learning from rigid doctrinal instruction into a living, transformative spiritual and ethical experience.

items.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

items.title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
items.abstract: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). Data selection, participation, integration, and preprocessing in different tasks result in many virtual datasets [Khan et al., SSC 2026]. Meanwhile, different users need to discover existing virtual datasets frequently and easily to avoid duplicate efforts. To enable an effective search engine in a DVS, it is desirable to automatically generate keywords for each virtual dataset. In this work, we present a solution for generating keywords for virtual datasets using large language models (LLMs). We propose five strategies for selecting different collections of text data for processing by the LLMs. We applied the five strategies to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets. We conducted experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques. The experiments show that the performances of the five strategies depend on the quality of the text descriptions. The results help us adopt a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service (KGS) as part of an extended DVS. The work demonstrates that the capability of automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume DVS that is dataset-rich and frequently accessed.

items.title: Autonomous Collaborative Robotics in Drone Swarms: Advanced Control Strategies for Complex Environments
items.abstract: Drones that can fly around on their own in groups are really good at watching things, helping with disasters, and doing work in factories. They have a hard time working together, scaling up, and changing what they do when things get complicated. When one person or computer is in charge of all the drones, it takes too long to make decisions. When the drones make their decisions, they have a hard time not running into each other and saving energy. So, we made a way for drones to work together using artificial intelligence. This way uses various kinds of learning and lets the drones make their own decisions. We tried this way with computers, and it worked really well. The drones got better at working, did things faster, finished tasks, and did not run into each other as much, even when there were a lot of things in their way.

items.title: Backlash of AI Monitoring: Untangling the Cause of Counterproductive Work Behavior in Construction Projects
items.abstract: Abstract While the ubiquitous adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) monitoring in construction projects has substantiated significant gains in operational efficiency and safety, its backlash remains theoretically underdeveloped. In practice, AI is gradually replacing human supervisors to monitor workers’ operation trajectories and work status. However, existing research has not yet unpacked workers’ cognition and behavioral responses toward AI monitoring. Therefore, grounded in the combination of psychological reactance theory and social exchange theory, the current study investigates how AI monitoring triggers counterproductive work behaviors and the boundary role of perceived organizational support. Through a survey of 352 on-site workers across diverse engineering projects, our findings reveal that AI monitoring is positively correlated with both production and political deviance. This relationship is mediated by negative cognition and anger, while perceived organizational support serves as a critical moderator that mitigates these detrimental effects. Furthermore, combined with the two supplementary studies, this research further verifies that the AI monitoring context triggers reactance among on-site workers when they perceive threats to freedom. By uncovering these distinct underlying mechanisms, this study extends the application of psychological reactance theory to the research context of AI monitoring on on-site workers in construction projects and develops a context-specific explanation.

items.title: Balancing the Efficiency–Validity Trade-Off
items.abstract: Abstract The history of education, both in terms of teaching and of assessing students, is one of ever-increasing scope and breadth, with constant pressure on educators to do more, with more students, using as few resources as possible. For this reason, much of the practices associated with modern educational measurement (e.g., multiple-choice items) have been designed with efficiency in mind, rather than psychological validity. Today, generative artificial intelligence (AI) promises to yet-again increase the efficiency of education, by outsourcing some tasks typically done by human educators to AI. One area where AI has already been consistently applied is in the psychoeducational assessment of creative thinking, where AI appears to be able to score student responses to human-written tests, assemble assessment batteries of existing tasks, and even possibly write new assessments itself. In this chapter, we discuss the increase in efficiency that AI can bring to creativity assessment, while also considering how this increase in efficiency might exacerbate or even generate new validity issues, especially vis-à-vis the societal consequences of assessing the creativity of students from diverse cultural backgrounds and perspectives, using the same AI evaluator.

items.title: Barriers and Facilitators to the Implementation of Electronic Prescribing Systems in Healthcare: A Systematic Review Using a Sociotechnical Framework
items.abstract: Background: Electronic prescribing (e-prescribing) and computerized provider order entry (CPOE) are increasingly used in medication management, but successful implementation depends on more than technology. How systems fit workflows, user practices, organizational conditions, and the policy environment can influence their use in routine care. Objective: To synthesize empirical evidence on barriers, facilitators, and other factors influencing e-prescribing/CPOE implementation in clinical practice. Methods: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed and Scopus were searched for empirical studies published from January 2000 through December 2025. Eligible studies directly examined barriers, facilitators, determinants, or implementation processes involving e-prescribing, CPOE, EPMA, or EMMS in clinical settings. Methodological quality was assessed at criterion level using MMAT 2018 without an overall numerical score. Results: The review included 49 reports representing 48 unique studies. Workflow disruption and workload were most frequent (46/48; 95.8%). Technical infrastructure/usability, perceived usefulness/safety/efficiency/time, acceptance/resistance/self-efficacy/trust, and leadership/organizational readiness/user engagement were each identified in 45/48 studies (93.8%). Training and implementation support occurred in 43/48 (89.6%), communication/interoperability/prescription processing in 38/48 (79.2%), and policy/financial/external-environment factors in 21/48 (43.8%). Conclusion: E-prescribing/CPOE implementation involves interconnected technical, workflow, human, organizational, and external factors. Workflow fit, organizational readiness, user involvement, implementation support, and policy and resource conditions require attention when systems are introduced or optimized. Theme frequencies indicate study-level presence rather than effect estimates.

items.title: Barriers to professional mental health help-seeking and considerations for school-based interventions among Secondary School adolescents: an exploratory qualitative study
items.abstract: ABSTRACTProfessional mental health service use remains low among adolescents, and school-based interventions are frequently designed without consulting the young people and clinicians they are intended to serve. This exploratory qualitative study investigated the specific barriers to professional mental health help-seeking among Nigerian adolescents to inform the development of a culturally relevant school-based intervention. Following the ethical principles of the Belmont Report, a focus group discussion was conducted with ten secondary school students (aged 13–16), alongside individual in-depth interviews with two students and key informant interviews with two practicing clinical psychologists in Ibadan, Nigeria. Audio-recorded transcripts were verified and examined utilizing thematic analysis. Eight core categories emerged from the data, highlighting a limited formal understanding of mental health among youth and a prominent gap between baseline knowledge and help-seeking behaviors. While distress including depression, anxiety, addiction, and trauma was widely recognized through behavioral or academic declines, pervasive stigma and the fear of diagnostic labeling acted as dominant barriers to care, with nine out of ten adolescents refusing professional care pathways. Friends served as primary confidants, while parental spiritual beliefs heavily gatekept formal psychological interventions. Social media heavily informed adolescent self-image but introduced acute body-image concerns. Notably, one student preferred using an artificial intelligence chatbot over human contact to ensure absolute confidentiality. Participants requested foundational mental health literacy and coping skills delivered via brief, visual, interactive sessions, while clinicians anticipated systemic institutional implementation challenges regarding school leadership, funding deficits, and staffing constraints. Interventions must target social stigma and privacy constraints directly alongside conceptual awareness.

items.title: Becoming creative cyborgs: What role(s) for GenAI in the creative writing classroom?
items.abstract: This article reports on my action research study exploring the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing pedagogy at higher education level. Over twelve months, I conducted six pedagogical experiments across three London institutions, engaging fifty-two students in exploring AI’s functional dimensions: as ideation catalyst, collaborative tool, scaffolding mechanism, editorial assistant, research facilitator and assessment instrument. Using a critical realist framework, I examine what emerged from this systematic investigation: GenAI demonstrates clear affordances in particular contexts (research, translation, ideation generation) but significant limitations in others (editorial feedback, assessment, true creative collaboration). Students across all cohorts showed sophisticated critical awareness of AI’s training processes and ethical implications, and most remained cautious about deploying AI as a creative tool. The article argues that engaging with GenAI’s weaknesses might be its greatest pedagogical strength.
